newsitem.title: USA: Chase Manhattan, Citicorp profits up in quarter.
newsitem.headline: Chase Manhattan, Citicorp profits up in quarter.

text.p: Chase Manhattan Corp. and Citicorp, the two largest U.S. banking companies, Tuesday reported strong quarterly earnings that were in line with expectations, boosted by improvements in their key businesses.

Chase Manhattan, the largest U.S. bank in terms of assets, said it earned $927 million in the first quarter, including restructuring costs related to its merger with Chemical Banking Corp. in March 1996.
This compared with a loss of $89 million in the year-ago quarter, which included a merger-related after-tax charge of $1.03 billion and $70 million in special items.
Operating net income rose 9 percent to $946 million from $867 million in the 1996 first quarter.

Chase reported fully diluted earnings per share of $2.01, before merger-related restructuring costs, up 11 percent from $1.81 in the first quarter of 1996. Primary earnings per share rose to $2.02 from $1.82.

"First-quarter earnings reflect the benefits of Chase's balanced business portfolio, with key wholesale and retail areas contributing solid results," said Walter V. Shipley, chairman and chief executive officer.

"While revenue growth in the quarter was lower than our 1997 target, financial performance continues to be strong, as demonstrated by the significant improvement in the efficiency ratio and a higher return on equity."
Total revenue in the first quarter was $4.15 billion, which included a $44 million gain on the sale of a non-strategic foreign investment, compared with $4.04 billion in the ygo quarter.
In a sign of possible consumer credit problemad, Chase said its credit card charge-off rate rose to 5.66 percent, compared with 5.11 percent in the fourth quarter and 4.66 percent a year ago.
Expenses fell 2 percent, reflecting merger savings of $205 million and underlying growth of 6 percent, Chase said.
Citicorp, the second-largest banking company, said its net income rose 9 percent to $995 million, or $2.01 a share, in the first quarter despite continued weakness in U.S. consumer credit.
This compared with $914 million, or $1.75 a share, in the year-ago period.

"We are accelerating our plans to get fully engaged in our business directions, to offset continuing weakness in the U.S. consumer credit environment plus the need to fund the expansion of our franchise in the emerging markets and the globalization of our processing base," said John Reed, Citicorp's chairman.
"We expect to end 1998 fully engaged in our business strategy, with the improved momentum implied by it."
The loss ratio in Citicorp's U.S. credit card business rose to 5.91 percent in the quarter from 5.45 percent in the 1996 fourth quarter and 4.38 percent in the 1996 first quarter, Citicorp said.
The increase in net income and the rise in the U.S. credit card loss ratio were close to Wall Street expectations.

Citicorp said its consumer businesses, including its branch banking, credit card business and private bank, earned $490 million in the first quarter, a decline of 3 percent from the 1996 first quarter.

Citicorp said the primary factor in the decline in consumer business was a 14 percent decrease in card earnings, partly offset by improved earnings in the consumer banking business. The consumer businesses had adjusted revenue of $3.5 billion, up 7 percent from the 1996 first quarter.
Chase's stock rose $2.25 to $92.75, while Citicorp gained $3.125 to $109.625 on the New York Stock Exchange in early trading.
